label: Separation Theorems
notes: Open by making separation the engine rather than a technical appendix. The claim is that a hyperplane can become evidence: it certifies disjointness, supports a boundary point, or turns an infeasible primal statement into a dual object. Point students to the normal vector and the two ordered support numbers.

label: Hyperplane Certificates
notes: Treat a separating hyperplane as a compact certificate rather than just a drawing. To verify it, one does not inspect every point visually; one checks the ordered support values induced by the same normal. Flipping the normal only swaps the two sides, so the mathematical content is the signed ordering.

label: Proper Separation
notes: Pause on the word proper because it is easy to overread it as positive margin. Proper separation still permits equality of the two support numbers. Its job is to rule out a useless certificate where both convex sets are entirely inside the same hyperplane and the normal has detected no real side information.

label: Strong Separation With Distance
notes: Separate strict language from strong language. Strict inequalities say the points are on open opposite sides, while strong separation records a positive numerical gap in the support values. The nearest-pair argument is the most memorable construction because the vector between closest points becomes the certificate normal.

label: Supporting Hyperplanes
notes: Explain support as one-sided contact. A supporting hyperplane is allowed to touch a face, an edge, or a single exposed point, but it must contain the whole set in one closed half-space. The support-function equation is a useful bridge to the next sections on conjugacy and dual representation.

label: Point Outside A Closed Convex Set
notes: This is the most concrete theorem in the lecture. Closedness gives a nearest point, convexity turns the nearest-point condition into an obtuse-angle inequality, and that inequality is exactly the separating hyperplane. The positive distance from y to C becomes the positive margin in the certificate.

label: Disjoint Convex Sets
notes: Use this slide to organize the family of theorems. The difference-set trick explains why disjointness can be studied as point separation from a convex set. Then distinguish the conclusions by strength: weak ordering, proper nondegeneracy, and strong positive gap require different hypotheses and should not be merged in memory.

label: Relative Interior Qualification
notes: This is the conceptual centerpiece. The theorem says that proper separation is exactly controlled by relative interiors, not by ambient interiors. Stress why this matters for lines, faces, and affine slices: a lower-dimensional convex set can have empty ordinary interior while still having a rich relative interior.

label: Farkas Preview
notes: Do not try to prove Farkas fully here; use it as a preview of the duality pattern. The important lesson is the alternative structure: either a primal representation exists, or a hyperplane normal certifies impossibility. That normal will later be called a multiplier, a dual variable, or a subgradient.

label: Projection Proof Picture
notes: Walk through the proof from the picture instead of from formalism alone. The nearest point creates a right-angle condition against every feasible direction inside the convex set. Expanding the squared distance along a segment gives the variational inequality, and the inequality is already the separating half-space.

label: Numerical Separator Solver
notes: Connect the theorem to a practical workflow. A convex optimizer can propose the closest pair or a maximum-margin normal, but the lecture should insist on the last line: verify the support inequalities. This is the computational version of proof hygiene, because a candidate normal is not a certificate until the margins are checked.

label: Failure Without Closedness
notes: Use this example to keep students from upgrading every separation statement to a strong one. The open half-space and the boundary point are disjoint, but the distance is zero because the set approaches the point. A weak supporting line exists for the closure, yet no positive margin certificate can be valid.

label: Duality Foreshadowing
notes: Frame this as the bridge out of Section 11. The normal vector in separation becomes many later objects depending on notation: a multiplier, a subgradient, a polar vector, or a conjugate slope. Students should leave seeing duality as organized certificate extraction rather than as a separate algebraic trick.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Read the ledger as a proof checklist. Before invoking a separation theorem, identify the kind of conclusion required and then verify the corresponding hypotheses. This prevents the two common errors: using a strong separator when only proper separation is justified, and forgetting relative interiors for lower-dimensional convex sets.

label: Recap
notes: Close with an inspection routine rather than a slogan. A separation proof should always identify the sets, the normal, the support values, the margin, and the exact existence hypothesis. That routine makes the section useful immediately for Farkas alternatives, support functions, conjugates, and the duality arguments that follow.
